title: Is Hole N" The Rock haunted? Paranormal team says it contacted the couple who built it
excerpt: Is Hole N the Rock haunted? A Utah paranormal team ran a spirit box session at the cave home south of Moab and says it reached the Christensens.
content:
It would be reasonable to suspect that the cave house at Hole N” The Rock, south of Moab, is haunted just by the decor. The excavated dwelling, carved into a sandstone cliff, is dark and full of porcelain dolls and busts of dead presidents. Still not convinced? Take a look at the taxidermied rigor mortis horse in the corner. Or the life-sized portrait of Jesus Christ in the living room. Did I mention that the original owners are buried out back?

Nothing about the property, which is also a petting zoo, is normal. But is there anything paranormal happening here?

According to a team of ghost hunters who performed a seance at the house on Saturday night, yes. The Utah-based group Paranormal Seekers Adventures believes it made contact with Albert and Gladys Christensen, the couple who built Hole N” The Rock starting in the 1940s.

“We had a lot of responses,” says Clinton Hansen, who used a device called a spirit box, which the team says picks up voices from the other side, during the investigation. “I was surprised how much activity there was. All very positive.”

A spirit box is essentially a radio scanner that rapidly shuffles through AM and FM frequencies. On Saturday, Hansen and another team member, Kassandra Klas, listened to the devices through headphones and repeated any fragments of speech they could pick up on the scanner. Whatever they said was interpreted as answers to questions that were being asked aloud to the spirits by other team members while Klas and Hansen were channeling. To ensure Klas and Hansen couldn’t hear the questions and rig their answers, they wore blindfolds and noise-canceling headphones.

The session with the spirit boxes took place in the alcove where the Christensens are buried. Klas and Hansen sat side by side, hand in hand, and rocked slowly back and forth as they called out words. A cameraman filmed the scene with infrared equipment — the group publishes its findings on its YouTube channel — while the rest of the team and a few Hole N” The Rock employees gathered around.

When team leader Janell Cook asked a question about maintaining the historic house, which opened to public tours after Albert’s death in 1957, Hansen spontaneously said: “Blaine will help.”

All looked at Blaine Reniger, a local historian who was watching the session. Reniger has done preservation work at Hole N” The Rock previously and intends to resume that process this winter.

“Coming into the night, I was kind of a skeptic,” he says. “But once they said that, I started to think maybe something else was going on here. I have a very uncommon name, and these people didn’t know my name.”

Reniger later recounted times when he had felt some kind of presence in the house while working. In one example, he was cleaning a lapidary saw that belonged to Gladys when he heard a noise behind him. He turned and saw that his box of cleaning supplies had been opened.

He remembers telling what he believes was the ghost of Gladys that he was just there to clean the saw, which was a beloved object of hers.

“Then there was this feeling like someone was in the room laughing, and I just laughed too,” he says. “The encounters are always friendly like that.”

“It makes sense that Albert and Gladys would still be there,” Reniger continues. “They poured so much work into that home, and it’s pretty much exactly how they left it. Some things haven’t moved in 70 years.”

“In a lot of ways, it’s still theirs,” he says.
